entry.title: Pinball Illusions – The Vikings table arrives on the Amiga AGA via PC {AI WIP}
entry.content:
Well, here's some interesting news for the weekend, as the elusive fourth table, The Vikings, is unofficially making its way to the Amiga A1200 (AGA). While the original 1995 release of Pinball Illusions famously included only three tables on the Amiga, the PC version was fortunate enough to receive the Norse-themed addition. Now, thanks to a dedicated developer by the name of MrDig, with the help of Claude AI to migrate the PC data, the table is being converted to run natively on the original Amiga engine. The port integrates into the classic menu as a proper fourth selection, complete with its own dedicated high-score list, menu picture, and custom info text.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

The project has already achieved a small milestone, with full gameplay proving highly stable on both physical A1200 hardware and the FS-UAE emulator. Packed using Imploder to save valuable chip RAM, the conversion successfully runs all core mechanics, including the dot-matrix ship mini-game, Thor and Labrador multiballs, and end-of-ball bonuses. While the table is fully playable via hard-disk installation and WHDLoad, the developer is currently polishing the remaining animations, synchronising the audio with the PC original, and exploring an optional feature to centre the game screen on modern monitors.

  • Via the sourced linked forum thread you will find table4 bin files you can place in the WHDLoad version "PinballIllusions v2.2 AGA". See the readme.txt for instructions. Expect bugs, and do report them (preferably screenshots/videos of the bugs) so I can feed those to claude and make it better.

entry.title: Fix it Felix Jr - Another fabulous Arcade port, but this time for the Amstrad CPC Plus by Amstrad GGP!
entry.content:
The Amstrad CPC Plus and GX4000 gets a surprise addition to their ever growing software libraries with the release of Fix it Felix Jr, a stunning homebrew arcade game developed by Amstrad GGP. Based on the fictional arcade game featured in the 2012 animated movie series, this project brings a modern pop-culture myth to life on the Amstrad hardware. Players step into the shoes of the iconic repairman, Felix Fixe Junior, who must scale a shifting building to repair windows shattered by the frustrated giant, Ralph.... "GONNA WRECK IT!"

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Capturing the authentic spirit of the 1980s golden age, the gameplay delivers pure, fast-paced arcade action across multiple floors. As you climb, you must dodge falling bricks and hazardous birds while utilizing Felix's magical golden hammer to fix the damage. Along the way, players can collect medals and eat delicious pies left on windowsills by grateful tenants. Developed as a dedicated fan game, this release perfectly bridges the gap between cartoon fiction and retro reality for Amstrad owners across the globe.

entry.title: Amiga 1942 - The Amiga gets a smooth scrolling Arcade port from retrodnagames!
entry.content:
Well, here's a Sunday surprise! As Retrodnagames has released a fan-made port of Capcom’s legendary 1984 arcade shooter 1942! This impressive homebrew project brings the classic vertical shoot-'em-up to the Commodore Amiga with an uncompromising, old-school ethos. Retrodnagames has coded the entire game from the ground up using AsmOne assembly language, painstakingly rebuilding all 32 stages, enemy flight patterns, and maps from scratch simply by studying arcade gameplay videos. Proudly crafted entirely by hand without any AI assistance, the port achieves decent performance too, boasting vibrant 32-colour graphics that run at a silky-smooth 50 frames per second at a native 224x256 resolution.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

This ambitious release aims to honor the legacy of the original arcade smash hit designed by Yoshiki Okamoto, which originally served as the foundational entry in Capcom's iconic 194X franchise. Set in the Pacific Theater of World War II and loosely based on the historic Battle of Midway, the game uniquely tasks players with fighting their way to Tokyo to dismantle the enemy air fleet—a design choice originally tailored to capture Western markets that helped the game become a massive global financial success in the mid-1980s (wiki). This definitive Amiga tribute includes every single enemy type from the original cabinets, all the classic power-ups, and there's even a few hidden surprises!

Minimum System requirements:

  • OCS PAL Amiga. Runs on ECS and AGA as well
  • Floppy version: 512K chip mem, and 512K any mem
  • HD version: 512K chip mem, and 1Mb any mem. WHDLoad 17+

entry.title: Amiga Outrun AGA - Retrodnagames works his magic on a classic Arcade racer for the Amiga!
entry.content:
The Amiga news is coming in thick and fast, as now we welcome the release of 'Outrun AGA', an ambitious fan-made reimagining of Sega’s legendary arcade racer built to replace the notoriously poor official Amiga port from back in the day. Developed by retrodnagames, this project is coded entirely from the ground up in old-school assembly language. Steering clear of modern shortcuts, the developer proudly avoided any form of generative AI during creation to hopefully ensure an authentic arcade experience. Built to squeeze every ounce of power from original, 1993-era Commodore hardware, the racing title is purely blitter-driven, requiring a PAL-based AGA Amiga equipped with a standard 68020 CPU and 4MB of fast RAM. Because of its specialized reliance on native Amiga custom chips, faster modern processor upgrades won't alter the game's execution speed.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Outrun Amiga, Yeh it's that bad!


▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Amiga Outrun AGA - Music seems a little glitchy, may be emulator related!


This impressive technical feat perfectly honours the spirit of Yu Suzuki's iconic 1986 masterpiece. This native Amiga recreation packs in all 15 stages bringing the complete journey to life in a crisp 320x224 fullscreen resolution. Visually anchored by a striking 32-colour display mode running at a steady 25 frames per second, the game delivers beautiful sprite-scaling action that mirrors the coin-op original. Players can cruise to all three original music tracks while simultaneously listening to robust three-channel sound effects, keeping the immersive premium stereo experience intact. Best of all, Amiga owners can lock in their best runs with high scores saved directly to a hard drive across every distinct difficulty setting.


Minimum System requirements:


  • AGA PAL Amiga with 4Mb fast RAM. Runs full speed on 68020. This is intended to run on close to original 1993 C= hardware. Since the game is blitter driven, faster CPU's will not make it run faster.

entry.title: Wipeout 2097/XL - A Playstation hit futuristic racer gets an Amiga AI port, albeit beefy Amiga's required!
entry.content:
Welcome to Wipeout 2097/XL, a native AmigaOS 3 port rebuilt entirely from a source decompilation of the original PlayStation code. Coded by Arcziii (arczi84) with the help of AI, this non-commercial port relies on modern hardware expansions, requiring an Amiga system running PiStorm with a Raspberry Pi 3, 4, or CM4 under Emu68. To handle the high-octane 3D performance, your setup must feature RTG with a 32-bit screen mode, roughly 64 MB of free RAM, and an active AHI sound subsystem. Players can choose between two specialized render versions depending on their software setup: xl-ogles using the ogles2.library with MSAA support, or xl-minigl utilising minigl.library v29. Performance tests show that the MiniGL build provides an extra boost, clocking in at roughly 10 frames per second faster. 

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

If you've got the power, then this release offers Amiga owners the definitive way to experience one of the greatest video games of all time. Centered around the iconic F5000 AG racing league, the game challenges players to pilot blazing-fast, weapon-equipped futuristic crafts across gravity-defying global race tracks. Wipeout originally defined mid-90s gaming culture, praised heavily by critics for its distinct visual aesthetic, alongside its ground breaking licensed soundtracks featuring artists like The Chemical Brothers and The Prodigy. Wipeout 2097 even received critical acclaim upon release; reviewers praised the game for its dramatic improvements to the controls, graphics, and gameplay of the original Wipeout (Wiki).

  • You will need to provide your own original Wipeout XL USA PlayStation retail disc (SCUS-94351) or a corresponding digital .bin/.cue image, as the download contains no copyrighted game data. Helpfully, the package does include NR74W's beautiful HD texture pack—originally created for DuckStation—which completely overhauls the in-game HUD, fonts, weapons icons, and title screens with modern high-resolution fidelity.
  • Caffeine OS has an RTG version of Wipeout included, but even that version with a Pistorm ran incredibly slowly or didn't start at all.

[

entry.title: Aces of the Pacific - An MS-DOS combat flight sim by Dynamix gets a PC modernization
entry.content:
On this Remembrance Sunday, I thought it would be worth mentioning that the legendary MS-DOS combat flight simulator Aces of the Pacific, has un-officially received a modern PC port. Dubbed Aces of the Pacific: Enhanced, this project was developed by Kylofon through reverse-engineering with the help of AI. While completely revitalizing the classic with upgraded modern performance and improved visuals, the new native version faithfully preserves the magic of Dynamix’s original 1992 masterpiece. For many players, the classic title originally published by Sierra On-Line was the definitive World War II Pacific Theater flight simulator, even outclassing heavyweight contemporary rivals like 1942: Pacific Air War.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

The modernized release allows a new generation of players to dive into the historic aerial conflicts of World War II. True to the original, players can pilot individual single missions or embark on extensive career modes, choosing to fly for the United States Navy, Marines, or Army Air Forces, or take to the skies for the Imperial Japanese Army or Navy. By bridging the gap between the nostalgia of the MS-DOS version and modern PC hardware, Kylofon's project honors the legacy of Dynamix—who famously followed up this landmark simulation with Aces Over Europe in 1993—giving aviation enthusiasts a seamless way to revisit one of the most influential flight games ever made.

Features

  • Smooth 3D view at your display's refresh rate.
  • High resolution (up to 2560 × 1600) with anti-aliasing; optional 16:9 widescreen.
  • Three times the view distance, the finest aircraft and ship models at every distance.
  • Distance haze, a smooth sky and a soft horizon.
  • Held direction keys combine (Left + Down pulls through a turn).
  • Separate flaps down and flaps up keys.
  • A launcher with key bindings.

Requires the CD-ROM version 1.2 of Aces of the Pacific (it includes WWII: 1946). The floppy releases (1.0, 1.01, 1.2 / Patch B and the 1946 expansion disk) don't run: they are separate builds of the game. The launcher and the game say which version a folder holds. A copy is at the Internet Archive: download AcesotP.zip and use the files of its AcesotP\DYNAMIX\AOTP folder.

Kirby2000 has set his sights on another classic game, as he has released a brand-new unofficial conversion of The Great Giana Sisters for the ZX Spectrum. While a version of the classic platformer was originally reviewed by magazines back in 1988, it was abruptly withdrawn from production before ever hitting store shelves, leaving no known surviving copies. This anticipated release finally fills that decades-old gap in the microcomputer's speccy library, giving fans a chance to experience the legendary title on the ZX Spectrum as if it was released all those years ago by Time Warp with publishing by Rainbow Arts.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube


▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

The ambitious port is a rather decent recreation, packing all 33 original stages of platforming action alongside secret bonus rooms and hidden warps. Players can hunt down eight distinct power-ups, compete for the top spot on a high-score table, and enjoy flexible joystick support covering Kempston, Sinclair, and Cursor setups (with custom key mapping also available). Aside from a multiload version  for 48K speccies, the release even features a fully functional two-player mode, breathing new life into a lost piece of gaming history.

entry.title: Vallation - A 2016 Cybernoid style game for the ZX Spectrum has been enhanced for 128k
entry.content:
Moving away from the C64, we now look towards the enhanced release of 'Vallation', a thrilling ZX Spectrum 128k Cybernoid style game developed by Sokurah. Transporting players deep into outer space, this title tasks brave pilots with navigating a nimble spaceship through a heavily guarded enemy complex in a desperate bid to escape a hostile pirate planet. Heavily inspired by the classic Cybernoid, the game challenges players to survive across a sprawling labyrinth where they must dodge laser barriers, avoid incoming fire, and outmanoeuvre indestructible missiles.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

This expanded 128k edition via itch io is far more than a simple port, delivering a massive overhaul based directly on community feedback. The adventure has grown exponentially, boasting double the visual tiles and three times the enemy variety scattered across its levels. Sokurah has completely rewritten the mechanics—introducing better-looking projectiles and easier-to-kill foes—while adding a high-score table, dedicated 128k audio, and Kempston joystick support. While the core game features 101 intense screens spread over four levels, players will also discover a massive, non-linear fifth level. Adding another 49 screens to bring the total to 150, this final maze plays out like Sabre Wulf in space, requiring players to hunt for vital pickups scattered across multiple branching paths to unlock the final escape teleporter.

entry.title: Robocop Arcade - Ranx is working on an Arcade-like version of Robocop for Amiga 500 {AI}
entry.content:
The Commodore Amiga community has just been treated to a bit of a tease, with the reveal of RoboCop Arcade, a brand-new conversion of Data East’s legendary 1988 coin-op developed by Ranx with the help of AI. While the original Amiga port of the era often left fans wanting more, this  project aims to recreate the arcade game's authentic 1:1 visuals and raw gameplay feel on the humble, unexpanded Amiga 500 OCS. Built strictly around the machine's base hardware—including a stock Motorola 68000 processor and a tight 512 KB of RAM—the game aims to have hardware scrolling, Blitter-driven sprites, and all nine action-packed stages, including the iconic target-shooting bonus ranges.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Fitting an arcade-accurate experience onto a standard setup does require a lot of optimization, culminating in the entire game being packed onto a single 880 KB floppy disk. Ranx managed this through aggressive resource compression, sophisticated multi-stage loading systems, and meticulous memory management, leaving a mere 1,536 bytes of free space remaining on the disk. Amiga owners can even look forward to a classic "cracktro" sequence upon booting, alongside digitized speech and sound effects that make full use of the Amiga’s four-channel Paula audio chip. As this impressive passion project continues to evolve, the developer is actively seeking community feedback to fine-tune what is shaping up to be the definitive retro tribute to an arcade classic.

entry.title: Insector X - An unofficial AI fan port of Taito's 1989 horizontal shooter by caiusarcade {WIP}
entry.content:
Caiusarcade has just released an early build of an unofficial fan port of Taito's 1989 horizontal shooter Insector X for the Commodore Amiga. Rather than building a remake from the ground up, this  conversion uses static recompilation to translate the original arcade machine's dual Z80 processors straight into native 68020 code. Every piece of game logic, artwork, and audio is pulled straight from the coin-op original, with the developer and the full use of AI assistance verifying the translated code frame by frame and matching the Amiga display pixel by pixel against the arcade release.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

To get this arcade-accurate insect blaster running, you will need an Amiga 1200 (or another AGA based machine) equipped with a hard drive, Kickstart 3.x, around 1.3 MB of free chip RAM, and at least 4 MB of fast RAM, though 8 MB is ideal. While a stock 14 MHz 68020 keeps the gameplay and music running at full speed with a lower refresh rate during hectic moments, stepping up to a 50 MHz 68030 or faster delivers faster performance throughout most of the action. Setting up the game is also straightforward if you have the ROMS, as users can compile the build using a simple one-click tool on Windows 10 or 11, or put it together on Linux and macOS using Python 3 and vasm.

- Please note the Audio seems to be broken in the video which may be early beta related

entry.title: AcidBoutique - A new music tool for the Commodore Amiga, a 303 bassline synth and a 808 drum machine!
entry.content:
On the topic of music and not retro gaming, here's a new piece of software called AcidBoutique, a  music production tool for the Commodore Amiga created by solo developer wintermute303. Built in the developer's spare time with the help of AI, this software squeezes the authentic sound and feel of two iconic electronic instruments—the TB-303 bassline synthesiser and the TR-808 drum machine—onto a classic 40-year-old Amiga 500 with just 1 MB of RAM or more. Instead of relying on rough approximations, the software is the result of reverse-engineering, running the genuine logic of the original hardware in real time on the Amiga's Motorola 68000 processor so that every slide, accent, and drum hit behaves just like the real deal.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

It is the kind of studio setup bedroom producers would've probably liked to have had back in the 1990s. Because of copyright restrictions however, Amiga users will need to supply their own original 303 and 808 ROMs to get started, with full instructions tucked inside the manual. Priced at roughly the cost of a single cup of coffee, wintermute303 is offering the tool to the community in hopes that a little support will help fund future updates for this music development tool.

entry.title: Blue Max: Megadrive Remake - A fan remake of Blue Max, the 1983 World War I flight game!
entry.content:
Here's a new Sega Mega Drive game, it's the 'Blue Max: Megadrive Remake', a homebrew project from developer gerla.cc. Drawing direct inspiration from Peter Adams’ Commodore 64 port of Bob Polin’s 1983 World War I classic, this version preserves the original game's core world and mechanics while giving them a modernized megadrive overhaul. Players are put back in the cockpit of a classic biplane, soaring over rivers, roads, and bridges to bomb enemy tanks, ships, and buildings while dogfighting rival aircraft. Between bombing runs on the enemy city, you will need to touch down on friendly airfields to refuel, repair damage, and restock your ammunition as you work your way up from a lowly Kamikaze Trainee to the prestigious rank of Blue Max.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

To take full advantage of the Mega Drive and Genesis, gerla.cc rebuilt the game from the ground up to run at a smooth 60 frames per second, introducing a fresh perspective alongside visuals rendered directly from 3D models. The remake also offers plenty of flexibility for both newcomers and seasoned veterans of the 1983 original, featuring three distinct difficulty tiers—Beginner, Advanced, and Expert. Additionally, players can tailor the flight physics to their liking by toggling gravity on or off and switching between Normal and Pilot control schemes, making it easier than ever to jump right in and have a blast.

entry.title: Aonic - HOT NEWS as Sonic the Hedgehog gets an early v2 demo on the Amiga and it's impressive! [UPDATE]
entry.content:
Well this is incredible news, and one I didn't expect for a bank holiday Monday. As a classic gaming icon has made a surprising leap over to the Commodore Amiga 1200 as a highly anticipated work-in-progress demo of Sonic the Hedgehog. Titled as Aonic and released by reassembler, this impressive technical feat ports the blue spinning hedgehog over from the Sega Mega Drive to the Amiga. This project over the many months of development, has captured the attention of Amiga retro gamers eager to see how Sega's flagship title performs on the Commodore A1200 hardware.

The underlying engine relies directly on the original Mega Drive source code, utilizing the comprehensive disassembly published by the Sonic Retro team. Because it shares this foundational DNA, the homebrew port plays identically to its console counterpart, preserving the precise physics, momentum, and speed that defined the 1991 classic. However, because the remainder of the game is still being implemented, certain aspects of the performance and design could still improve or degrade before a final release.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

NEW DEMO GAMEPLAY WITH AUDIO SOON


Translating the game to the Amiga required significant engineering adjustments because the two systems are very different pieces of kit, despite sharing a similar 68000-based CPU. Specifically, hardware like the Amiga 1200 struggles with bus contention when moving large amounts of data around—a hurdle that is easy to circumvent when designing an Amiga game from scratch, but highly problematic when porting an existing title at high quality. To overcome this, the rendering engine was heavily optimized and rewritten for the Amiga, resulting in some necessary visual differences while keeping the gameplay intact. You can see all the deviations from the Megadrive Version (HERE)


[UPDATE] Reassembler has officially released the second playable demo for Aonic (Sonic The Hedgehog). This latest version brings the ambitious port closer to a finished game by adding full music and sound effects. The release follows a thorough round of hardware testing that successfully cleaned up several performance bugs. Developer reassembler also credited artist Ric for providing valuable help with the project's visual artwork. Work is already moving fast on the next stages of the game. Creating the initial Green Hill Zone took the developer about 12 months of difficult groundwork. However, progress on the upcoming Marble Zone is moving much quicker. This new level will only take about four weeks to port. The faster timeline is possible because the custom optimization tools built during the first year of development are fully reusable.
